version: Lecture notes dated November 1997; local supplementary PDF, 10 pages

topic_relevance.basis: The supplementary lecture notes prove the maximum-volume inscribed ellipsoid theorem, its symmetric improvement, sharpness, and uniqueness.

definitions: A convex body is a compact convex subset of R^n with nonempty interior.
The John ellipsoid is a maximum-volume ellipsoid contained in the convex body.
For a centrally symmetric body, the center may be taken at the origin.

assumptions: K is a convex body in R^n.
theorem_cards.statement: There is an ellipsoid E with center c such that E subset K subset c+n(E-c). The dilation factor n is sharp.
proof_steps: Parameterize ellipsoids as AB^n+b; the feasible parameter set is compact and |det A| is continuous, so a maximum-volume ellipsoid exists.
Use an affine change of variables so the maximizing ellipsoid is B^n and its center is 0.

For a point p in K with |p|=a>n, let C_a=conv(B^n,p) and define the affine flow Psi_t(x,y)=(−1+e^t(x+1),e^(−lambda t)y). In two dimensions the moving circle stays in the tangent wedge for small t when lambda>1/(a−1); symmetry gives containment in higher dimensions.
The volume is multiplied by e^((1−(n−1)lambda)t). Since a>n, choose 1/(a−1)<lambda<1/(n−1); this strictly increases volume while staying inside K, contradicting maximality.
A simplex example shows n cannot be reduced.
theorem_cards.author_claim: The theorem and sharpness are stated by the author.
theorem_cards.checked_derivation: I read all ten pages. I rendered PDF pages 5 and 7 and verified the OCR-sensitive thresholds lambda>1/(a−1) and, in the symmetric proof, lambda>1/(a^2−1). The determinant factor e^((1−(n−1)lambda)t) and interval choices then give the stated contradictions.
theorem_cards.transfer_inference: The factor n is valid without symmetry; it cannot be replaced by sqrt(n) unless the body is centrally symmetric.

assumptions: K is a convex body in R^n symmetric about the origin.
theorem_cards.statement: There is a centrally symmetric maximum-volume inscribed ellipsoid E such that E subset K subset sqrt(n) E; the factor sqrt(n) is sharp for the cube.
proof_steps: Normalize the maximal ellipsoid to B^n and take p=(a,0,...,0), together with -p.
Use the symmetric linear flow (e^t x,e^(−lambda t)y); the contact-point slope condition is lambda>1/(a^2−1).
The determinant gain remains e^((1−(n−1)lambda)t); if a>sqrt(n), choose 1/(a^2−1)<lambda<1/(n−1), contradicting maximality.
For [-1,1]^n, B_2^n is the John ellipsoid and the vertex has Euclidean norm sqrt(n), proving sharpness.
theorem_cards.author_claim: The symmetric John ellipsoid inclusion and cube sharpness are stated by the author.
theorem_cards.checked_derivation: I visually checked the extracted theorem and the flow threshold on page 7. The inequality a^2>n is precisely what makes the interval for lambda nonempty.
theorem_cards.transfer_inference: Use this normalization only after central symmetry is established; an arbitrary convex body gets factor n instead.

assumptions: K is a convex body in R^n: compact, convex, and with nonempty interior. The proof uses convexity of the feasible affine images AB^n+b.
theorem_cards.statement: The maximum-volume inscribed ellipsoid of K is unique.
proof_steps: Represent each ellipsoid as AB^n+b with A positive definite by polar decomposition.

The feasible set of pairs (A,b) is convex. The determinant inequality det(A+B)^(1/n)>=det(A)^(1/n)+det(B)^(1/n), with equality only for proportional positive-definite matrices, forces two maximizing ellipsoids to have the same matrix.
If their centers differ, their convex hull contains a translate-centered ellipsoid with strictly larger volume, contradicting maximality.

For distinct centers, affine-normalize the common maximizing shape to B and the centers to ±a e1 (a>0). Then conv((B−a e1)∪(B+a e1))=B+[-a,a]e1 contains the centered ellipsoid with semi-axes sqrt(1+a^2),1,…,1. For a point (x,y) on this ellipsoid with x>=a, the squared distance to the segment [-a,a]e1 is at most (x−a)^2+1−x^2/(1+a^2), whose maximum on [a,sqrt(1+a^2)] is at an endpoint and is <=1; for |x|<=a the distance is ||y||<=1, and the x<=−a case is symmetric. The ellipsoid therefore lies in the convex hull and has strictly larger volume, a contradiction.
theorem_cards.author_claim: Theorem 3 states uniqueness; the determinant inequality and center argument are proved in the notes.
theorem_cards.checked_derivation: The determinant/Minkowski inequality step was checked. The center contradiction is also checked by normalizing the equal-shape ellipsoids to unit balls at ±a e1 and verifying that the ellipsoid with first semiaxis sqrt(1+a^2) and remaining semiaxes 1 lies in their convex hull; its volume ratio is sqrt(1+a^2)>1. The original displayed proof gives this containment geometrically in Figure 7 but not the distance calculation.
theorem_cards.transfer_inference: A claimed canonical John ellipsoid is unambiguous for each convex body, though an algorithm still needs to compute it.
gaps: Theorem 3 is stated using “compact body”; its proof explicitly requires K to be convex. Read the claim with the convex-body hypothesis from the lecture notes. A merely compact nonconvex set, such as two disjoint unit balls, can have two distinct maximum-volume inscribed ellipsoids.

The source has an apparent typographical slip in the proof of Proposition 4.2 where P^{-1}AP^{-1} appears in the determinant expansion; the surrounding definition and subsequent substitution use C=P^{-1}BP^{-1}. The evidence card follows the corrected algebraic identity.

constant_dependence: The nonsymmetric dilation is exactly n; the centrally symmetric dilation is exactly sqrt(n). Both are sharp. The affine-flow proof's positive determinant exponent requires lambda<1/(n−1), while containment imposes the lower threshold stated above.
endpoint_limits: K must be full-dimensional, compact, and convex; the argument is for convex bodies in finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
The sqrt(n) conclusion requires central symmetry about the chosen origin.
The result concerns a maximum-volume inscribed ellipsoid. A Löwner ellipsoid is the minimum-volume circumscribed ellipsoid and requires a separate polarity or dual-body argument.
This is distinct from John domains, John--Nirenberg inequalities, and Loewner differential equations.
reusable_methods: Affine-normalize an extremizer before estimating the containing body.
Prove sharp dimension constants by a local volume-improving deformation and the exact containment threshold.
Separate existence, inclusion, sharpness, and uniqueness into distinct proof obligations.
Check OCR-sensitive formulas against rendered PDF pages when a constant controls whether the parameter interval is nonempty.
unchecked: The notes cite John's original result and prior expositions but the arguments recorded here are the self-contained proofs presented in the ten-page lecture note.
